newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: European labour bosses visit Seoul strike leaders.
newsitem.headline: European labour bosses visit Seoul strike leaders.

text.p: In a gesture of international worker solidarity, European labour leaders on Saturday visited South Korea's strike headquarters in a ramshackle tent on the grounds of Seoul's Catholic cathedral.
Their visit highlighted mounting overseas criticism of South Korea's new labour law, which has sparked two weeks of nationwide strikes.
The law allows worker layoffs and replacement of striking workers and limits freedom of worker association by continuing to recognise just one union umbrella body.

Marcello Malantacchi, secretary general of the International Metalworkers' Federation, and Guy Rider, who heads the Geneva office of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU), attacked the bill as an assault on fundamental rights.
"What we're doing here is adding to worldwide reaction against the offensive by the Korean government on human and trade union rights," Rider said.
"It is very rare that an attack on unions brings the type of international reaction that we have seen here."
He called on the South Korean government to begin dialogue with labour unions to resolve the crisis.
Malantacchi called the law a "step backwards".
"We hope the government will understand it is for the good of this country to bring labour legislation into line with international standards," he said.
Arrest warrants have been issued for seven leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions camped out in the snow at Myongdong Cathedral.
Workers wielding steel pipes have so far protected them from police trying to seize them.
Under the new law the usually pliant Federation of Korean Trade Unions will enjoy a legal monopoly on union representation until 2000.

South Korea has become more vulnerable to international attacks on its labour policies since it joined the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) in December with a pledge to implement legal reform.
OECD chief Donald Johnston said on Friday he was worried about the turmoil and had reminded Seoul's envoy in Paris of the organisation's commitment to human rights.
An OECD statement said Johnston, at his first meeting with the new South Korean envoy, had expressed the concern and dismay of other members. The OECD would review the law on January 22.
OECD members have previously protested against the imprisonment in South Korea of union leaders.

"The Korean government undertook to reform its legislation in line with internationally accepted standards, including such basic rights as freedom of association and collective bargaining," the statement added.
The head of the International Labour Organisation wrote to South Korean President Kim Young-sam this week after the ICFTU asked him to intervene to prevent Seoul arresting strike leaders.

ILO spokesman Michel Barton told reporters in Geneva on Friday that freedom of trade unions was a fundamental principle of the United Nations agency, which promotes basic workers' rights in its 174 member states.

South Korea, which joined the ILO in 1991, has twice been reprimanded by an ILO committee for arrests of trade unionists and non-recognition of trade unions in violation of ILO principles of freedom of association.
